claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has an inherent ferritic-pearlitic microstructure.
High-temperature exposure enhances atomic mobility and diffusion.
Temperatures of at least 700 °C provide sufficient thermal activation for the proposed diffusion processes.
Enhanced diffusion at high temperature produces rapid inward oxygen diffusion and outward iron diffusion in Q235 steel.
High-temperature salt exposure forms a coherent, dense, adherent iron-oxide scale on Q235 steel.
The protective high-temperature scale is likely magnetite-rich or spinel-type.
A dense and coherent high-temperature oxide scale slows subsequent salt-induced corrosion.
At room temperature, lower diffusion kinetics produce a discontinuous, porous, and less protective oxide film on Q235 steel.
The porous room-temperature oxide film leads to higher local corrosion rates under chloride-salt exposure.
Q235 steel exposed to chloride salt at 800 °C will have lower mass loss and corrosion rates than Q235 steel exposed at room temperature.
The 800 °C specimens will show greater oxide-phase uniformity, continuity, density, and adhesion than room-temperature specimens.
The proposed protective effect should not occur at room temperature because oxide-scale formation is kinetically limited.
The proposed protective effect should not occur in the absence of an oxidizing atmosphere.
A controlled test should compare identical Q235 specimens exposed to NaCl for about 1000 hours at 800 °C and room temperature while controlling oxygen partial pressure.
Mass measurements, XRD, SEM, and adhesion testing can distinguish the predicted corrosion and scale characteristics.
Failure of the 800 °C samples to develop a denser, more coherent scale with lower corrosion than the room-temperature samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.
The exact protective-oxide phase fractions and quantitative corrosion improvement for Q235 under these conditions are not established.
